scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define JSON and why programs share it.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: **JSON** is a text format for structured data.
Almost every programming language can read it.
Many weather, payment and delivery services answer in JSON.

segments.say: JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for structured data: dictionaries, lists, text and numbers, inside each other.
Almost every language can read it. So many weather, payment and delivery services answer in JSON.

scenes.title: The idea: JSON text and Python data
scenes.direction: Teach the type table, the two directions, the API conversation and the analogy. Quiz on null. Breather.

segments.say: JSON looks almost like a Python dictionary, but it is text. A JSON object becomes a dictionary.
An array becomes a list.
A string becomes a string. JSON allows only double quotation marks.
True and false are written in small letters. And null is JSON's word for nothing.

visual.heading: Two directions
visual.label: The idea
body: `json.dumps()`: data to text. `json.loads()`: text to data.
visual.pre:
Python data           json.dumps()         JSON text
  {"vegan": True}   ------------------->  '{"vegan": true}'
                    <-------------------
                         json.loads()

segments.say: The json module translates in both directions. Dump s turns Python data into JSON text. Load s turns the text back into data.
Read the S as string. Without the S, dump and load work with a file instead.

visual.heading: How a web API answers
visual.label: The idea
body: A **web API** is a service that other programs can ask for data.
visual.pre:
Your program                        Weather service
  REQUEST:  GET https://api.example.com/weather?city=Riverside  -->
                         <--  RESPONSE: status 200 OK
                              body: {"current": {"temp_c": 31.5}}

segments.say: A web API is a service that other programs can ask for data. Your program sends a request to a web address.
The service sends back a response. The status code says how it went: 200 means OK, and 404 means not found.
The body holds the data, usually as JSON. Many services also want an API key: a secret password for programs. Keep it out of your code, and out of AI chats.

visual.question: What does JSON `null` become in Python?
visual.explain: `null` is JSON's word for nothing, and Python's word for nothing is `None`.

segments.say: Quick check. What does JSON null become in Python?

after.say: D. None. Null and None both mean: nothing here.

items: JSON is text for structured data.
`dumps` makes text. `loads` makes data.
An API answers with a status code and a body.

visual.heading: Step 3: JSON that people can read

segments.say: Step 3. Line 4 holds a drink with an accent: Café au lait.
Lines 6 and 7 add two settings. Ensure ascii equals False keeps every letter as it is. Indent equals 2 puts each value on its own line.
Line 5 has no settings. Look closely at the accent in Café.

ask.question: How does line 5 write the word `Café`?

after.say: As a code: C a f, then backslash u 0 0 e 9. By default, dump s writes every character outside basic English as a code. The data is still correct, but hard to read.
Line 6 keeps the real letter. Line 7 also indents, two spaces for each level.

items: `dumps` and `loads` work with strings.
`dump` and `load` work with files.
`ensure_ascii=False` keeps accents.

scenes.title: Step 5: A saved API response
scenes.direction: Show the illustrative live call, then why programmers save a sample. Show the sample. Ask what line 7 prints. Reveal.

visual.heading: Step 5: Asking a real service
visual.label: Build it
body: On your own computer, the standard library can send the request.
visual.pre:
# illustrative: api.example.com is a placeholder
  import json
  from urllib.request import urlopen

  url = "https://api.example.com/weather?city=Riverside"
  with urlopen(url) as response:
      print(response.status)
      data = json.load(response)

segments.say: Step 5. On your own computer, a program can ask a real service for data. The url lib module, from the standard library, sends the request.
An error status, such as 404, makes url open raise an H T T P error, which try can catch.
This address is a placeholder. Live answers change every minute, so programmers save one real response as a file, called a sample response, and test on it.

scenes.title: Work with AI: reading a supplier's prices
scenes.direction: Safety first. Six stages on price_of. Generate treats a list as a dictionary. Test catches text prices. Debug handles null. Improve invents a field.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: explain a response
visual.label: Before you start
items: Paste a sample response, and ask for its structure.
Check every field name and path against the real sample.
Never paste an API key or private customer data.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: paste a sample response, ask the AI to explain it, then check every field name against the real sample.
And never paste an API key, or private customer data.
Here is the supplier's saved response, prices dot json. Look closely at each price.

messages.text: Here is a saved response from my milk supplier's price service. Do not write code yet. Describe its structure, level by level. Which values are text, and which are numbers?

The response is an object with supplier, currency and items.
items is a list. Each entry is an object with name, price and unit.
Every price is text in quotation marks, such as "1.20", not a number.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha pastes the sample, and asks for its structure, level by level. No code yet.
The AI says items is a list, and every price is text in quotation marks. Asha checks the sample: both are true.

messages.text: I wrote price_of myself. Do not rewrite it. What does it return for milk, and which line handles an item that is missing?

For milk it returns 1.2, a float, because line 9 converts the text.
Line 10 returns None when no name matches.
I ran it for milk and for flour:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes her own price of first. It loops over the list, and converts the text with float.
The AI says milk gives 1.2, and line 10 handles a missing item.
She runs it. Milk gives 1.2, and flour gives None. Her version works.

messages.text: Write price_of(data, name) for this response. It returns the price of the named item as a number. What does it return for milk?
Here it is. For milk, it returns 1.2.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. To compare, Asha asks the AI for the same function, and what it returns for milk.
The AI writes one line, and says: milk gives 1.2.

visual.heading: The AI's version, on the sample

segments.say: Look at line 7. It asks items for milk, by name. Remember what items is in the sample.

ask.question: The AI says this returns `1.2` for milk. Is it right?

after.say: No. A type error. Items is a list, and a list needs a number as its index, not the name milk.
That is what list indices must be integers means. The AI treated the list as a dictionary of names.

messages.text: Your code stopped with a TypeError: list indices must be integers. Fix it. Then give me test cases with the exact value I should get.

Here is a version that loops over the list.
Cases: milk gives 1.2, oat milk gives 1.85, and flour gives None.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha reports the error, and asks for test cases with exact values.
The AI's next version loops over the list. And it lists three cases: milk, oat milk, and flour.

visual.heading: The three cases, on the AI's loop

segments.say: Line 9 returns the price. Line 20 prints each result with exclamation r, so text shows its quotation marks.

after.say: No. It got 1.20 in quotation marks: text, not a number. Text is never equal to the float 1.2.
Only flour passes. Plan said every price is text, and the AI forgot its own words.

messages.text: Two cases fail: you return '1.20' as text. Explain why, then fix it.

This supplier sends every price as a string. The return line gives it back unchanged.
Fix: return float(item["price"]).

segments.say: Asha shows the AI the failing cases, and asks why.
The supplier sends prices as strings, so the return line must convert them with float.

visual.heading: The three cases, after the fix

segments.say: She runs all three cases again. All pass.

visual.heading: Stage 5: the next day's response
visual.note: prices_today.json: oat milk is out of stock, and its price is null.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. The next day, oat milk is out of stock, and the supplier sends null as its price. Milk still works. Oat milk crashes on line 9.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: Today's response has null as the oat milk price. My code crashed on the return line with: TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a real number, not 'NoneType'. Explain the cause first. Then show the smallest fix.

JSON null becomes None in Python, and float(None) raises a TypeError.
Fix: before the return line, check for it:
if item["price"] is None: return None.

segments.say: Asha pastes the error, and asks for the cause first.
JSON null became None, and float of None is a type error. The fix checks for it with is None, from step 2.

visual.heading: All four cases, on the final function

segments.say: Lines 9 and 10 are the fix. She adds the new response as case 4, on line 19, and runs every case again. All four pass.

messages.text: All four cases pass. Suggest one improvement, with one reason. Use only field names that are in my sample.
Read item["unit_price"] instead of item["price"]. It is the standard field for the price of one unit, so the code is clearer.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one improvement, using only field names from her sample.
The AI suggests unit price, and calls it the standard field.
Asha's rule: every field name must appear in the sample. Lines 9 and 11 read unit price.

ask.question: Will this run on Asha's sample?

after.say: No. A key error. The sample has price and unit, but no unit price. The AI invented the field.
So Asha keeps her final function.

visual.heading: Her final function, one more run

segments.say: She runs her four cases one more time, on her own function. All four pass.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistakes 1 and 3 are spot-it asks. Mistakes 2 and 4 are explained.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 1. You try. Line 4 holds some JSON text. Line 5 loads it.

after.say: The text uses single quotation marks. Python accepts both kinds, but JSON accepts only double ones.
after.heading: Mistake 1: single quotation marks

after.say: The report runs through the json module's own files. On your computer, these lines show full file paths. Skip to the last line: column 2 is the first single quotation mark.

segments.say: Mistake 2. Dump writes into a file, so it needs one: F P is the file parameter. To get a string, use dump s.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Lines 4 and 5 read scone dot json. Line 6 asks for the item.

after.say: No. Read text gives a string, not a dictionary. A string accepts only number indexes.
after.heading: Mistake 3: text is not data

after.say: The fix: turn the text into data first, with load s.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: number keys come back as text

segments.say: Mistake 4. JSON object keys are always strings. The table numbers 1 and 2 came back as the text 1 and 2.
Asking back for key 1 is a key error. Use string keys from the start.
